anatomy.intro: This drawing follows the visible obesa-type form without claiming a confirmed pure species.

parts.function: The rounded rib is part of the succulent body.
parts.label: Fleshy rib

parts.function: Purple-brown markings cross the grey-green stem; they are coloration rather than separate leaves.
parts.label: Transverse band

parts.function: Small sites near the upper rib crests can produce cyathia, the characteristic Euphorbia flower clusters.
parts.label: Flowering eye

parts.function: The upper growing region continues the rib pattern as the body develops.
parts.label: Crown

flowers.text: Euphorbia flowers are grouped into tiny cyathia rather than cactus-like petaled trumpets. Pure obesa has separate male and female plants; that reproductive pattern should not be assumed for Dragon’s Egg without observing its flowers.

growth.note: Species illustrations are a useful comparison, but the hybrid’s mature form and sex remain unconfirmed.

stages.text: The obesa-type body begins as a compact ball.
stages.title: Rounded youngster

stages.text: The stem enlarges while keeping its strongly grooved outline.
stages.title: Developing ribs

stages.text: Pure obesa elongates with age; an unknown hybrid may branch or develop differently.
stages.title: Older form

habitat.text: The wild obesa species comes from the Great Karoo near Graaff-Reinet in South Africa’s Eastern Cape. Its rounded, stone-like body belongs to a drought-adapted spurge, not a cactus. Dragon’s Egg is recorded here as an obesa-type hybrid or selection with unknown parentage, so that South African setting describes its apparent ancestry rather than a verified hybrid origin.

image.alt: Obesa-type Euphorbia showing numbered fleshy rib, transverse color band, small flowering eye and central crown; no cactus areoles.

An obesa-type Euphorbia hybrid sold as Dragon's Egg: compact rounded grey-green succulent ball, eight broad vertical ribs with muted transverse purple-brown bands. Hybrid parentage is unknown so do not exaggerate pure-species details. 1 points to broad fleshy rib; 2 to a transverse purple-brown band; 3 to a tiny brown flowering eye near an upper rib crest; 4 to the central growing crown. lookalikes.name: Monk’s hood cactus
lookalikes.text: A ribbed shape is shared, but Astrophytum has woolly areoles bearing spines. This Euphorbia’s tiny flowering sites are different structures; do not injure the plant to test for latex.

mature.text: SANBI describes pure obesa to about 20 cm high and 9 cm wide. Those figures offer a comparison scale, not a promised final size for a plant with unknown parentage.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Altman Reserve.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: The cactus resemblance is an example of similar succulent shapes appearing in unrelated families. Euphorbia’s floral structure and milky latex reveal its very different botanical identity.
